title: Gather Victim Org Information: Determine Physical Locations
shortTitle: Gather Victim Org Information: Determine Physical Locations
summary: This sub-technique narrows organisation gathering to physical geography: where a victim's offices, data centres, warehouses, and key infrastructure sit, and which legal jurisdiction and authorities govern each site. That combination matters because it informs both physical and non-physical follow-on activity. Adversaries assemble addresses from contact pages, filings, licence records, and procurement notices, then enrich them with map and satellite imagery, delivery and shipping records, and staff photographs that show interiors, badges, or loading areas. The resulting knowledge supports hardware additions, supply chain interference, mail-based delivery of devices, impersonation of couriers, and jurisdiction-aware decisions about where to host infrastructure or how quickly law enforcement could respond. Detection lives mostly outside the network, in visitor and delivery logs, badge access records, closed circuit television (CCTV) review, and staff reporting of unusual interest in a facility, which means the discipline is about correlating physical events rather than reading packet captures.

beginner.definition: This sub-technique is about finding out where an organisation's buildings and equipment are. It includes offices, data centres, and warehouses. It also covers which country and legal rules the organisation answers to.
beginner.whyItMatters: Location details help an attacker in several ways. They can send hardware or letters to a real address. They can plan visits, deliveries, or theft. The country also matters, because laws and police powers differ from place to place. If you publish too much, these plans become much easier to make.
howItWorks: The attacker collects addresses from contact pages, public registrations, and official filings.
They look at staff posts that show office interiors, badges, or building names.
They match addresses with map and satellite images to find entrances and loading bays.
They check delivery firms and shipment records for where equipment is sent.
They note which country each site sits in, because that affects legal powers.
They use the details to plan a physical approach or a convincing delivery.
beginner.example: Imagine you want to send a parcel to a busy company. You want it to reach a person rather than the front desk. First you find the building address, which is easy and public. Then you learn which door the couriers use and when the office is quiet. You might read a staff photograph that shows the sign above the loading bay. None of this breaks any rule, and it simply makes your delivery more likely to succeed. Attackers collect physical locations in the same patient way. The risk is not the address alone, but the address combined with the daily routine around it.
takeaways: Physical addresses are public, so control who reaches the doors and when they may enter.
Check what staff photographs reveal about buildings, badges, and entrances.
Record and review visitor and delivery logs, because physical approaches leave traces there.

objectives: Explain why physical location data is collected and how it supports later adversary activity.
Identify open sources that disclose office, data centre, and warehouse addresses.
Describe how imagery, delivery records, and staff photographs enrich an address list.
Explain why legal jurisdiction is part of location reconnaissance.
Identify physical and procedural records that help detect interest in a facility.
